docs.title: wambatic
docs.text:
Statistics from github.com for a user, an organisation or a single repository, as a report in your terminal, as an HTML page with its assets folder, as JSON or in a web app on your own machine.

wambatic report repo:pallets/click --format html --by month

This reads the history of the repository from the GitHub API, keeps it in a local SQLite cache, writes one HTML file and prints its path. Open the file in a browser:

Note

Screenshots captured on 2026-11-11 from pallets/click and org:pallets with wambatic 0.1.0, covering 2024-11-01 to 2026-10-31.

The command needs a GitHub token. The GitHub token says how to get one in a minute.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
1. Install wambatic and get a token.
  2. Read Getting started for a first report, section by section.
  3. Read How wambatic works to see where the numbers come from.
  4. Choose what to report on with Targets and Periods and ranges.
  5. Choose how to see it: the terminal report, the HTML report, the web app or JSON output.
  6. Read what each group of metrics means: Activity, Flow, Delivery and DORA and Popularity.
  7. Look after the data and the settings: The cache, Configuration, Recipes and Troubleshooting.

The reference lists every option, setting and metric, and Limits says what wambatic does not do.

docs.title: Why wambatic
docs.text:
• One tool, four front ends. The same numbers appear in the terminal, in a page you can share with its folder, as JSON for scripts and in a web app.
  • Only what is new is fetched. After the first run, a sync reads the changes since the last one, so a repeat run is fast and a report from a warm cache works offline.
  • Nothing is hidden behind colour. Net lines carry a sign and a partial period carries a mark, so the output reads the same in a pipe or a screen reader.
  • Your token stays on your machine. It is never written to the cache, the logs or a report.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Only the default branch's history is read.
  • A report uses one time zone.
  • GitHub Enterprise Server is not supported.
  • The DORA figures are proxies, for trends rather than comparisons.
  • Watchers and languages are snapshots, not histories.

Limits gives each one with its reason.

docs.title: How wambatic works
docs.text: How data gets from GitHub to a report, and what limits how fast it goes.

docs.title: The pieces
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    gql[GitHub GraphQL API] --> fetch
    rest[GitHub REST API] --> fetch
    fetch[fetch<br/>sync what is new] --> cache[(SQLite cache)]
    cache --> stats[stats<br/>pure computation]
    stats --> terminal[Terminal report]
    stats --> html[HTML report]
    stats --> json[JSON]
    stats --> web[Web app]
  • fetch talks to GitHub: the GraphQL API lists repositories, commits, pull requests and issues, and the REST API supplies workflow runs, releases, stars, forks and the statistics endpoints. It writes what it reads to the cache.
  • The cache is a SQLite file. It is derived data: delete it and the next report rebuilds it. See The cache.
  • stats computes the numbers from the cache alone, with no network. That is why a report from a warm cache works offline.
  • The front ends render the same result: terminal, HTML, JSON and the web app.

docs.title: An incremental sync
docs.text:
The first sync of a repository reads its whole history. Later syncs read only what changed.

sequenceDiagram
    participant W as wambatic
    participant C as Cache
    participant G as GitHub
    W->>G: List the repositories of the target
    G-->>W: Names, last-push times, counts
    W->>C: Read the watermark for each repository
    Note over W: Nothing new in the listing: no request of its own
    W->>G: Fetch changes since watermark minus fetch.overlap
    G-->>W: New and changed rows
    W->>C: Store rows, move the watermark
    W->>G: REST request with the stored ETag
    G-->>W: 304 Not Modified (free) or a new body
    W->>C: Compute the report from the cache
  • The watermark is the time of the last sync of a resource. The next sync starts a little before it, by fetch.overlap, so an item that arrived late is not missed.
  • Conditional requests. For the REST endpoints wambatic keeps the ETag GitHub sent. Asking again with it costs nothing against the rate limit when nothing has changed.
  • Full refreshes. An incremental sync cannot see a deletion, so a resource is read in full again once fetch.full_refresh_after has passed since its last full read. --full-refresh forces it.

docs.title: Rate limits
docs.text:
GitHub limits how many requests a token may make: see the REST rate limits and the GraphQL rate limits. When the limit is reached, fetch.on_rate_limit decides what happens:

  • wait (the default) sleeps until the limit resets and carries on.
  • fail stops with an error that gives the reset time.

fetch.workers sets how many repositories are fetched at once. More is faster and closer to GitHub's secondary limits, which wambatic answers by retrying up to fetch.max_retries times. GitHub's own failures (HTTP 500 to 504, a dropped connection, or a GraphQL reply that carries no data) are retried the same way, waiting a little longer each time.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
A first report on a real repository, read section by section, then the same data as HTML and JSON.

You need wambatic installed and a token.

wambatic report repo:pallets/click --by month

The first run reads the whole history of the repository and may take a while for a large one; later runs fetch only what is new. The screenshots below were made with all four metric groups, which you ask for with --groups activity,flow,delivery,popularity; the default is activity,flow, so your first report has fewer sections. See Delivery and DORA and Popularity for why the other two are off by default.

Note

Screenshots captured on 2026-11-11 from pallets/click and org:pallets with wambatic 0.1.0, covering 2024-11-01 to 2026-10-31.

docs.title: The title and the activity table
docs.text:
The first line names the subject, the date range, the period and the time zone. Activity by period gives, for each period, commits, contributors, active days, and lines added, deleted and net. A Total row ends the table when there is more than one period. A period that the range cuts short ends in *; the caption under the table says so. See Activity and Periods and ranges.

The flow, delivery and popularity tables follow in the full report; The terminal report shows each section.

docs.title: Trends
docs.text: With more than one period, Trends draws a sparkline for each metric that has a value in every period, cropped to the width of your terminal, with the lowest and highest value beside it. Below it, Top contributors lists the first rows only; the JSON output has every row.

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text:
The last section says where the data came from: when the report was computed, when each resource was last fetched, and the wambatic and cache schema versions. Read it when two reports disagree: the fetch times tell you which one saw newer data.

Metrics whose inputs are not in the cache appear under Unavailable, with the reason, in place of a table.

Nothing in the output depends on colour: net lines carry an explicit sign, and partial periods carry a mark.

docs.title: Run it again
docs.text:
wambatic report repo:pallets/click --by month

The second run syncs again, because fetch.max_age defaults to zero, but a repository with nothing new costs almost nothing. To skip the network altogether, use the cache alone:

wambatic report repo:pallets/click --no-fetch

or sync only when the cache is older than a day:

wambatic report repo:pallets/click --max-age 1d

The cache explains how these choices interact.

docs.title: The same data as HTML and JSON
docs.text:
open "$(wambatic report repo:pallets/click --format html)"
wambatic report repo:pallets/click --format json | jq '.series[0].points'

The first command writes one HTML file and prints its path, so the shell can open it. The second prints a JSON document and nothing else on stdout, so jq can read it. See The HTML report and JSON output.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: How to install wambatic from a clone of its repository and check that it runs.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.14.7 or a later 3.14 release. uv can install it for you.
  • uv, which creates the environment and installs the dependencies.
  • git 2.40 or later, to clone the repository and, at run time, to read commits from bare clones of the repositories you report on.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/bnomis/wambatic
cd wambatic
uv sync
source bin/activate.sh
wambatic --help

uv sync creates .venv in the clone and installs wambatic and its dependencies there. source bin/activate.sh activates that environment and puts src on the Python path; run it in each new shell before you use wambatic.

docs.title: Check the install
docs.text:
wambatic --help lists the report, serve and cache commands. python -m wambatic runs the same program.

wambatic cache info

This describes the cache without changing it, and makes no request, so it needs no token.

docs.title: Shell completion
docs.text:
wambatic can print the completion source for your shell:

wambatic --completion generate

See the command line reference for the --completion option.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text:
git pull
git submodule update --init
uv sync

A cache written by an earlier wambatic may be refused after an upgrade. The cache is derived data, so run wambatic cache clear and the next report fetches it again; see The cache.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
What wambatic does not do, and why.

  • Only the default branch's history is read, unless you ask for more. Commits on other branches and unmerged work are not counted unless fetch.branches names them, for a repository that is cloned or read with fetch.api_history set to files.
  • A pull request's first review time can be missing. The first review is found among a pull request's first reviews on GitHub. When the author or bots leave more than a few before the first other reviewer, the other reviewer's review is not among them and the pull request has no review time. Reading every review of every pull request would cost many requests for a small gain.
  • Line counts are filtered only where wambatic can see each commit's files. A public repository, or one fetch.clone_repos allows, is cloned and its generated files are left out (stats.exclude_paths and stats.linguist). Any other repository keeps the default branch and unfiltered totals unless fetch.api_history is files, a slow per-commit read that applies stats.exclude_paths only. The report lists the repositories it could not filter. A repository's attributes are read at its default branch's head, and pull request sizes still include generated files.
  • Clones need disk space and git. Bare clones are kept beside the cache until wambatic cache clear.
  • Only cloned repositories carry author offsets. Periods are cut by the zone in --tz or stats.timezone. With --commit-tz author commits are dated in their authors' zones, but GitHub's API gives no offset, so only a repository read by clone has them. Any other commit is dated in the report zone unless stats.author_timezones names its author, and the report lists the repository as unavailable. See Periods.
  • Only some GitHub Enterprise servers are supported. Enterprise Server is supported from 3.19, as the guide describes. Enterprise Cloud with data residency (*.ghe.com) is not, because it uses different addresses.
  • The DORA figures are proxies. They are built on conventions GitHub does not enforce: what counts as a deployment, and which pull requests are fixes. See Delivery and DORA for the conventions and the settings that adjust them.
  • Watchers and languages are current snapshots, not histories. GitHub does not date them, so a report shows them as of the last sync.
  • The fork series count direct forks only. The fork count in Popularity now is GitHub's, which includes forks of forks, so the two can differ.

docs.title: The GitHub token
docs.text:
What token wambatic needs, how it finds it, and when it needs none.

wambatic reads GitHub through its API, which answers only requests that identify a user. That identity is a personal access token: a long string you create in your GitHub settings and that acts with the permissions you give it.

docs.title: The quickest way
docs.text:
If you use the GitHub CLI and have run gh auth login, there is nothing to do: wambatic asks gh auth token for the token. Otherwise:

export GITHUB_TOKEN=<token from https://github.com/settings/tokens>

docs.title: How the token is found
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    start([wambatic needs to call GitHub]) --> env{GITHUB_TOKEN set<br/>and not empty?}
    env -- yes --> use[Use it]
    env -- no --> gh{gh auth token<br/>prints a token?}
    gh -- yes --> use
    gh -- no --> fail[Stop with an error<br/>naming the fix]

A report that makes no request, with --no-fetch or a --max-age that the cache already satisfies, needs no token at all.

docs.title: A GitHub Enterprise Server
docs.text: For a host set with --github-host, wambatic never uses GITHUB_TOKEN; it looks for GH_ENTERPRISE_TOKEN, then GITHUB_ENTERPRISE_TOKEN, then gh auth token --hostname <host>. Run gh auth login --hostname <host> once to use the GitHub CLI. See GitHub Enterprise Server.

docs.title: What the token may do
docs.text:
wambatic only reads. Create a classic token or a fine-grained one.

Classic token (GitHub docs):

Scope Needed for public_repo Public repositories; enough for most uses repo Private repositories read:org Private membership of an organisation

Fine-grained token (GitHub docs), with read access to:

  • Repository permissions: Metadata, Contents, Pull requests, Issues and Actions
  • Organisation permissions: Members

A fine-grained token reaches only the repositories you select when you create it.

docs.title: What wambatic does with it
docs.text:
• The token is never written to the cache, the logs or a report.
  • A GITHUB_TOKEN that appears in an error message is replaced by ***.
  • The web app uses the token of the environment it runs in and never sends it to the browser.

docs.title: Activity
docs.text:
The commit, contributor and line metrics: what was committed, by how many people, and how much code.

wambatic report repo:pallets/click --by month --groups activity

activity is one of the default groups. Every metric is defined in the metrics reference; this page says what to watch for when reading them.

Metric What it tells you commits Commits on the default branch (and any fetch.branches you follow) in the period contributors Distinct commit authors in the period active_days Days in the period with at least one commit lines_added, lines_deleted, lines_net Lines changed by the commits in the period

docs.title: Merge commits
docs.text: commits counts merge commits. The line metrics leave them out by default, because a merge commit reports the lines of the branch it merges and they would be counted twice. Set stats.exclude_merge_commits to false to count them; it never changes commits. See Settings.

docs.title: Bots
docs.text: stats.bot_logins (by default dependabot[bot] and renovate[bot]) is left out of contributors and of the Top contributors table. A bot's commits still count in commits and in the lines, and the per-author breakdown from --by-author lists bots, because their lines are counted. Commits that GitHub cannot attribute to a login are not counted as contributors, since they cannot be told apart by person; the Top contributors table shows them as one unattributed row.

docs.title: Reading the numbers
docs.text:
• active_days is a count of days, not of commits: ten commits on one day make one active day.
  • lines_net is added minus deleted, and carries an explicit sign in the terminal.
  • Generated and vendored files are left out of the line counts where wambatic can see each commit's files (see How commits are read). A file is left out when its path matches stats.exclude_paths (lock files, vendor, node_modules, dist, minified files and source maps by default), or, with stats.linguist on, when the repository's .gitattributes marks it linguist-generated or linguist-vendored. The report footer says what the line counts leave out.
  • Only the default branch is read unless fetch.branches names more, so work on branches that was never merged does not appear by default.
  • A period is the date of the commit in the report time zone; see Periods and ranges.

docs.title: How commits are read
docs.text:
Each repository's commits are read by one of three methods, and the report footer names the methods used (Commits read by), the branches followed (Branches) and what the line counts leave out (Line counts leave out).

Method Footer label Used for Branches Generated files Clone local clone A public repository, or a private or internal one that fetch.clone_repos allows The default branch and those fetch.branches matches Left out API totals API totals Any other repository, when fetch.api_history is totals (the default) Default branch only Counted API with files API with files Any other repository, when fetch.api_history is files The default branch and those fetch.branches matches Left out by stats.exclude_paths only

A clone is a bare clone kept beside the cache (see The cache); it needs git 2.40 or later (see Installation).

To allow a private repository to be cloned, list it in fetch.clone_repos:

{
  "fetch": {
    "clone_repos": ["my-org/*"],
    "branches": ["main", "release/*"]
  }
}

Patterns use shell wildcards. fetch.api_history set to files reads one request per commit, so it is slow and uses much of the rate limit; choose it only for a repository you may not clone. Changing fetch.branches makes the stored commits stale: a report with --no-fetch or --max-age then stops with a BranchesMismatchError until you sync again.

docs.title: Unavailable rows
docs.text:
A repository that is read by API cannot be filtered fully. The report lists it under Unavailable, naming the repository and the reason:

  • lines_added, lines_deleted, lines_net: <repository>: generated files are counted, because the repository is not cloned and fetch.api_history is totals; or, with files, the linguist attributes were not read and only stats.exclude_paths applied.
  • commits: <repository>: only the default branch was read, though fetch.branches names more.

A repository's attributes are read at its default branch's head. Pull request sizes still include generated files.

docs.title: By repository and by author
docs.text: An organisation or user target adds a By repository table. --by-author adds a By author table, and per-author series in the JSON output. --by-author is an error for a user target. See Targets and The terminal report.

docs.title: The cache
docs.text:
Where the cache is, how it decides to sync, and how to inspect or clear it.

wambatic cache info

Screenshots captured on 2026-11-11 from pallets/click and org:pallets with wambatic 0.1.0, covering 2024-11-01 to 2026-10-31.

The cache is a SQLite file. It is derived data: everything in it can be read from GitHub again, so deleting it costs time and requests but loses nothing.

docs.title: Where it is
docs.text:
By default ~/.cache/wambatic/cache.sqlite3. Set fetch.cache_path in the configuration to move it. A leading ~ is expanded.

A host other than github.com has its own file, cache-<host>.sqlite3 beside it; see GitHub Enterprise Server. The cache records its host, and a cache made for another host stops the report with a CacheHostError. --ignore-cache-version does not override it: set fetch.cache_path to another file, or clear that host's cache.

docs.title: The clones
docs.text: A repository read by clone is kept as a bare clone in a clones directory beside the cache file, in a subdirectory named for the cache file. Set fetch.clone_dir in the configuration to keep them elsewhere. Clones can be large; cache info shows their size. They are derived data too: GitHub holds the same history. See Activity for which repositories are cloned.

docs.title: Older caches
docs.text: The cache records each cloned commit's author offset, which a cache made by an earlier wambatic lacks. It is refused with a version error: run wambatic cache clear and report again to fetch everything afresh.

docs.title: cache info
docs.text: wambatic cache info prints the path, the size, the identity the cache recorded (the schema version, the wambatic version and a hash of each query), every key that differs from the wambatic that is running (with both values), the size of the clones, what the cache holds for each kind of record, and when it was last synced. It reads the file without changing it, so it works on a cache that report refuses.

docs.title: cache clear
docs.text:
wambatic cache clear

This deletes the cache, its -wal and -shm files and the clones without asking. The next report fetches everything again.

docs.title: The version check
docs.text:
wambatic records which version wrote the cache and refuses to read one written by a different version, rather than mix results from two versions. The report then stops with a one-line error. You have two ways out:

  • wambatic cache clear, then run the report again. This is the usual choice: the cache is derived data.
  • --ignore-cache-version for one run. The override is recorded in the cache and shown as a warning in the report.

docs.title: Does a report sync?
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    start([wambatic report]) --> nf{--no-fetch?}
    nf -- yes --> skip[No sync: report from the cache]
    nf -- no --> fr{--full-refresh?}
    fr -- yes --> full[Read all history again, then report]
    fr -- no --> ma{fetch.max_age<br/>above zero?}
    ma -- no --> sync[Sync what is new, then report]
    ma -- yes --> age{Every resource synced<br/>more recently than max_age?}
    age -- yes --> skip
    age -- no --> sync
    sync --> old{A resource's last full read<br/>older than fetch.full_refresh_after?}
    old -- yes --> again[Read that resource in full again]
    old -- no --> inc[Read only what changed]
  • --no-fetch never touches the network and needs no token. It cannot be combined with --full-refresh, and a bare NAME target needs the network to resolve, so use user: or org: with it.
  • --max-age 1d (or fetch.max_age) skips the sync when the cache is recent enough. The default of zero always syncs.
  • A sync reads the repository listing, and a repository with nothing new in the listing costs no request of its own.
  • fetch.full_refresh_after (default 30d) is the age after which a resource is read in full again, which is the only way an item deleted on GitHub leaves the cache. A shorter value is more accurate and costs more requests.
  • --full-refresh reads all history again at once, for example after a force-push you suspect.

docs.title: What a first sync costs
docs.text:
The first sync with --groups delivery reads every workflow run of each repository, newest first, about one request for each hundred runs. The first sync with --groups popularity reads every star and every fork the same way. Later syncs ask for the newest page with a conditional request, which GitHub answers for free when nothing has changed, and read further only when something has. Releases are read again only when a repository's release count or newest release has changed.

See How wambatic works for the sync in detail and the rate limits.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
How settings are layered, where the file is, and what it looks like.

Most people never need a file: the defaults work. Write one when you pass the same option on every run.

mkdir -p ~/.config/wambatic
cat > ~/.config/wambatic/config.json <<'JSON'
{"stats": {"timezone": "Europe/Berlin"}}
JSON
wambatic report repo:pallets/click

docs.title: The layers
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    defaults[Built-in defaults] --> file[JSON file<br/>~/.config/wambatic/config.json<br/>or WAMBATIC_CONFIG]
    file --> flags[Command line flags]
    flags --> run([The settings of this run])

A later layer wins. Command line flags such as --tz, --format, --max-age and --out override the file for one run.

The file is ~/.config/wambatic/config.json. Set the WAMBATIC_CONFIG environment variable to use another file. A missing file named that way is an error, while a missing default file is not. The GitHub token is not a setting: see The GitHub token.

docs.title: An annotated example
docs.text:
{
  "fetch": {
    "workers": 8,
    "max_age": "1h"
  },
  "stats": {
    "timezone": "Europe/Berlin",
    "bot_logins": ["dependabot[bot]"]
  },
  "report": {
    "format": "json"
  }
}
  • fetch.workers: fetch eight repositories at once instead of the default. More is faster and closer to GitHub's secondary limits.
  • fetch.max_age: skip the network when everything was synced within the last hour.
  • stats.timezone: bucket periods in this IANA time zone unless --tz says otherwise.
  • stats.bot_logins: only this author is left out of contributor counts, so renovate[bot] now counts. A list replaces the default, it does not add to it.
  • report.format: print JSON unless --format says otherwise.

docs.title: Commit settings
docs.text:
These settings decide how commits are read and what the line counts include; the others are in the settings reference.

  • fetch.branches: branch name patterns followed beside the default branch. Empty (the default) follows the default branch only; ["*"] follows every branch.
  • fetch.clone_repos: owner/name patterns of private or internal repositories you allow to be cloned. Public repositories are cloned without it.
  • fetch.api_history: totals (the default) or files, for a repository that is not cloned.
  • fetch.clone_dir: where the bare clones are kept.
  • stats.exclude_paths and stats.linguist: which files the line counts leave out.
  • stats.commit_timezone: report (the default) dates commits in the report zone; author dates each in its author's zone unless --commit-tz says otherwise. See Periods.
  • stats.author_timezones: a JSON object from login to IANA time zone, such as {"octocat": "Asia/Tokyo"}. Logins are matched without regard to case, and an unknown zone stops the run before any sync. It applies in author mode and overrides the offset git recorded.

How commits are read says what each combination does. A list replaces its default, it does not add to it.

docs.title: Values
docs.text:
• A duration is a whole number and one unit, s, m, h, d or w, such as "30d".
  • A leading ~ in a path is expanded.
  • Booleans are JSON true and false.
  • An unknown section, an unknown key or a value of the wrong type is an error that names it, and wambatic exits with status 2.

Every setting, its type and its default are in the settings reference.

docs.title: Delivery and DORA
docs.text:
How a project ships: workflow runs, releases, and proxies for the four DORA keys.

wambatic report repo:pallets/click --groups delivery

delivery is not in the default groups, because it reads every workflow run of every repository. Use --groups activity,flow,delivery for everything but popularity. Every metric is defined in the metrics reference.

docs.title: Runs and releases
docs.text:
Metric What it is workflow_runs Workflow runs created in the period, whatever their state workflow_success_rate The share of completed runs that succeeded, shown as a percentage workflow_duration_p50, workflow_duration_p90 Minutes from a completed run starting to its last update release_count Releases published in the period, prereleases included, drafts left out release_interval_p50 Median whole days since the repository's previous release
  • The success rate counts only runs whose conclusion is success, failure, timed out or startup failure. Cancelled and skipped runs are not outcomes of the code and are left out of both counts.
  • The duration is an approximation: GitHub does not report a run's end time, so wambatic uses the time of the run's last update.
  • Runs triggered by pull requests are counted like any other.
  • A period without a completed run has no success rate or duration, and p50 and p90 are as in Flow.
  • For a user target, the runs and releases of the user's own repositories count, whoever made them.

docs.title: DORA proxies
docs.text:
DORA's four keys are deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service. GitHub records none of them, so wambatic estimates each from what it does record. They are proxies: use them to see a trend, not to compare teams.

DORA key Metric Deployment frequency deployments Lead time for changes lead_time_p50, lead_time_p90 Change failure rate change_failure_rate Time to restore service time_to_restore_p50, time_to_restore_p90

docs.title: What counts as a deployment
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    start[A repository in the report] --> set{stats.deploy_workflow set?}
    set -- yes --> run[A completed run of that workflow]
    run --> ok{Did it succeed?}
    ok -- yes --> dep[A deployment, at the time the run finished]
    ok -- no --> none[Not a deployment]
    set -- no --> rel[A published release]
    rel --> pre{Is it a prerelease?}
    pre -- no --> dep2[A deployment, at the time it was published]
    pre -- yes --> none

Deployments are counted for each repository. stats.deploy_workflow is matched against a run's workflow file name (deploy.yml) or its name. See Settings.

docs.title: Lead time
docs.text:
Lead time runs from a merged pull request's first commit (its creation, when that is not known) to the first deployment of the same repository at or after the merge. It is placed in the period of the deployment. A pull request that no deployment has followed yet is not counted.

gantt
    title Lead time of one pull request
    dateFormat YYYY-MM-DD
    axisFormat %d %b
    section Pull request
    First commit               :milestone, 2026-10-01, 0d
    Review and merge           :active, 2026-10-01, 2026-10-08
    Merged                     :milestone, 2026-10-08, 0d
    section Release
    Waiting for a deployment   :active, 2026-10-08, 2026-10-14
    First deployment after the merge  :milestone, 2026-10-14, 0d
    section Lead time
    lead_time, counted in the period of the deployment :crit, 2026-10-01, 2026-10-14

docs.title: Change failure rate and time to restore
docs.text:
A deployment has failed when a pull request of the same repository that carries a label in stats.hotfix_labels follows it within stats.failure_window (7 days by default). A deployment whose window is still open at the end of the range counts as not failed. Time to restore is the time from a hotfix pull request being opened to being merged, in the period of the merge.

gantt
    title A failed change
    dateFormat YYYY-MM-DD
    axisFormat %d %b
    section Deployment
    Deployment                 :milestone, 2026-10-01, 0d
    failure_window (7d)        :active, 2026-10-01, 2026-10-08
    section Hotfix pull request
    Opened with the label hotfix :milestone, 2026-10-03, 0d
    time_to_restore            :crit, 2026-10-03, 2026-10-04
    Merged                     :milestone, 2026-10-04, 0d

Here the hotfix was opened inside the window, so the deployment counts as failed.

docs.title: Unavailable metrics
docs.text:
Each proxy appears only when what it needs is in the cache; otherwise it is listed under Unavailable, with the reason. deployments and the lead time need at least one deployment. The change failure rate and the time to restore also need a pull request with a hotfix label. That is deliberate: a repository that never labels its hotfixes would otherwise show a change failure rate of 0%, which reads as good news and means nothing.

wambatic report repo:pallets/click --groups delivery --format json |
  jq -r '.tables.unavailable[] | "\(.metric): \(.reason)"'

For repo:pallets/click this prints that change_failure_rate and the two time-to-restore metrics have no pull request labelled hotfix. See JSON output.

docs.title: GitHub Enterprise Server
docs.text:
Read a GitHub Enterprise Server instead of github.com.

export GH_ENTERPRISE_TOKEN=<token created on your server>
wambatic report org:my-team --github-host ghe.example.com

The first report syncs from ghe.example.com, using its own cache file and its own token, and prints as any other report does.

docs.title: Set the host
docs.text:
Pass --github-host to report, serve or cache, or set fetch.github_host in the configuration to make it the default:

{"fetch": {"github_host": "ghe.example.com"}}

The value is a host name with an optional port, such as ghe.example.com:8443. wambatic reads the server's REST API at /api/v3 and GraphQL API at /api/graphql on that host. The default is github.com. api.github.com and *.ghe.com are refused.

docs.title: The token
docs.text:
An Enterprise host never uses GITHUB_TOKEN, so a github.com token is not sent to your server. wambatic looks for the token in this order:

  1. GH_ENTERPRISE_TOKEN
  2. GITHUB_ENTERPRISE_TOKEN
  3. gh auth token --hostname <host>, after gh auth login --hostname <host>

See The GitHub token for the scopes.

docs.title: The server version
docs.text: Before it syncs, wambatic asks the server for its version and stops with a one-line error if the version is older than the minimum, which is 3.19, or cannot be read. A report that makes no request does not check.

docs.title: One cache file per host
docs.text: A host other than github.com keeps its cache in ~/.cache/wambatic/cache-<host>.sqlite3, with : in a port written as -, so two hosts never share a file. The cache records its host and the server's version; wambatic cache info --github-host <host> shows both. A cache made for another host is refused even with --ignore-cache-version: see The cache.

docs.title: Rate limits that are switched off
docs.text: An administrator can switch rate limiting off, and the server then sends no rate-limit headers. wambatic syncs without them on an Enterprise host. On github.com a response without them is still an error.

docs.title: What is not supported
docs.text:
• GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency (*.ghe.com), which uses different addresses.
  • Servers older than the minimum version above.

docs.title: Flow
docs.text:
Pull requests and issues: how many are opened, merged and closed, and how long that takes.

wambatic report repo:pallets/click --by month --groups flow

flow is one of the default groups. The counts and times are defined in the metrics reference.

Metric What it is prs_opened, prs_merged Pull requests created and merged in the period issues_opened, issues_closed Issues created and closed in the period time_to_first_review_p50, time_to_first_review_p90 Hours from a pull request being opened to its first review time_to_merge_p50, time_to_merge_p90 Hours from a pull request being opened to being merged time_to_close_p50, time_to_close_p90 Hours from an issue being opened to being closed pr_size_p50 Median lines (added plus deleted) of the pull requests merged in the period

docs.title: Each event lands in its own period
docs.text:
An event is placed in the period of its own date in the report time zone, not in the period of the pull request's opening. A pull request opened in one month and merged in the next is in prs_opened for the first month and in prs_merged for the second, and its merge time is counted in the second.

gantt
    title One pull request across two months
    dateFormat YYYY-MM-DD
    axisFormat %d %b
    section Periods
    October                  :2026-10-01, 2026-10-31
    November                 :2026-11-01, 2026-11-30
    section The pull request
    Opened (prs_opened, October)             :milestone, 2026-10-28, 0d
    Open, waiting for review :active, 2026-10-28, 2026-11-02
    First review (time_to_first_review, November) :milestone, 2026-11-02, 0d
    Under review             :active, 2026-11-02, 2026-11-05
    Merged (prs_merged and time_to_merge, November) :milestone, 2026-11-05, 0d

So time_to_merge_p50 in November includes pull requests that were opened in October. A period in which nothing was merged has no point for it.

docs.title: Percentiles
docs.text: p50 is the median of the values in the period and p90 the 90th percentile: nine in ten values are at or below it. The median shows the usual case and the p90 shows the slow tail. A period with no value has no point (the terminal shows -), because a median of nothing is not zero.

docs.title: What is left out, and what is not
docs.text:
• Review time leaves out reviews by the pull request's author and by bots, so an automatic reviewer does not make every review time a few minutes. A pull request with no other reviewer has no review time.
  • Bots' own pull requests and issues are counted. stats.bot_logins only affects contributor counts; see Activity.
  • A closed, unmerged pull request counts only in prs_opened.
  • A reopened issue is open, so it is not in issues_closed.
  • A user target counts only the pull requests and issues that the user opened.

docs.title: The HTML report
docs.text:
A tabbed web page with tiles, charts and tables, beside an assets folder, that opens from disk.

open "$(wambatic report org:pallets --format html)"

The command writes one page and an assets folder beside it, and prints the page's path on stdout, so a script can capture it. The page has summary tiles, then a tab for each section (commits, contributors, lines, flow, delivery and popularity, for the groups you asked for). The tabs hold a chart for each measure, whole-range charts (top contributors, by repository and by author, and the languages), a calendar of commits by day, and the same tables as the terminal report, which you can collapse, sort, filter and export.

Note

Screenshots captured on 2026-11-11 from pallets/click and org:pallets with wambatic 0.1.0, covering 2024-11-01 to 2026-10-31.

docs.title: Light and dark
docs.text:
By default the page follows the viewer's light or dark setting and changes with it. Set report.html_theme to light or dark to fix it; see Configuration.

The charts use one colour set for each theme and never rely on colour alone.

docs.title: The tiles
docs.text: The tiles show the totals for the whole range.

docs.title: Switching period
docs.text: The page has a Year, Month, Week and Day switch. It does not need the network, or wambatic, to change the period: the page carries the data for every period. --by picks the period shown when the page opens (default month). --by total is an error here, because the tiles already show the totals.

docs.title: Partial periods
docs.text: A period that the range cuts short is hatched in bar charts, drawn with open markers in line charts, and named in the chart's caption. See Periods and ranges.

docs.title: The commit calendar
docs.text: A calendar of commits by day, one cell for each day of the range.

docs.title: Tabs
docs.text: The tab bar sits under the tiles. Click a tab, or use the left and right arrow keys, Home and End. The address of the page changes to name the tab (report.html#tab-flow), so you can send a link that opens on that tab. The tab ids are tab-commits, tab-contributors, tab-lines, tab-flow, tab-delivery and tab-popularity; a tab exists only for a group in the report. Without script, the tab bar is hidden and every section shows one after another.

docs.title: Tables
docs.text:
Every table is in a block you open and close by clicking its title. A table of more than ten rows starts closed, and its title says how many rows it holds.

  • Sort: click a column heading; click again to reverse, and once more to restore the original order. Numbers sort as numbers, not as text.
  • Filter: type in the box under a heading. A text column keeps rows that contain the text, ignoring case. A number column takes N or =N (equal), >N, >=N, <N, <=N, or A..B (from A to B, inclusive). A number may have , separators and a %. A box that matches none of these forms is marked as invalid and filters nothing. Filters on several columns must all match. The line under the table says Showing 37 of 412 rows, and the total row is marked Total (all rows) while a filter is on, because it is not the total of the rows shown.
  • Export: the CSV and Excel buttons under the table save the rows that are shown (sorted and filtered as you see them) with the headings. Numbers are written as numbers, and the CSV opens in Excel with non-ASCII names intact. A text cell that starts with =, +, - or @ gets a leading ' so a spreadsheet does not run it as a formula. A failed export shows one line and saves nothing.

docs.title: Where the files go
docs.text:
• --out PATH is a file, or an existing directory to write into. Without it the file goes in report.out_dir.
  • The file is named repo-OWNER-NAME.html, user-NAME.html or org-NAME.html.
  • The assets folder, wambatic-assets-HASH, is written in the same directory. Its name carries a hash of its contents, so a newer wambatic adds a folder beside an old one and never changes it, and every page loads the files it was made with. Reports written into one directory share a folder. An existing folder is reused only when its files are exactly the ones this wambatic writes; one that differs (edited, or put there by someone else) stops the run with cannot write PATH: it exists and does not hold this version's files; remove it, and no page is written.
  • Missing directories are created and an existing file is replaced.
  • The write is atomic: a failed write leaves the earlier file as it was, and no partial file. The folder is written first, so no page points at a folder that is missing.
  • --out is an error with another format.

docs.title: Offline and shareable
docs.text:
The page and its folder hold their own copy of plotly.js and make no request, so they open from disk and can be hosted together, for instance on GitHub Pages. The folder is megabytes in size for that reason.

Keep the page beside its folder. To send a report, send both, or zip them together; attaching the page alone to an issue loses the charts, tabs and styles. A page opened without its folder says so at the top: "This report's files (wambatic-assets-HASH) did not load; keep the page beside that folder." The tiles and tables still show, unstyled.

Per-period charts show the total series only. The breakdown by repository and by author is for the whole range.

docs.title: JSON output
docs.text:
The shape of the JSON document that --format json writes, and how to query it.

wambatic report repo:pallets/click --format json --since 2026-08-01 --until 2026-10-31 | jq '.series[0]'

The document goes to stdout and the logs to stderr, so a pipe sees only JSON. The web app's stats GraphQL query returns the same document; see The web app.

docs.title: An annotated example
docs.text:
This is a real document, cut down by hand: repo:pallets/click, --by month, --groups activity,flow, from 2026-08-01 to 2026-10-31. Elisions are marked ...; the keys and values shown are as written.

Note

Screenshots captured on 2026-11-11 from pallets/click and org:pallets with wambatic 0.1.0, covering 2024-11-01 to 2026-10-31.

{
  "format_version": 1, // (1)!
  "subject": {"kind": "repo", "login": "pallets", "name": "click"}, // (2)!
  "request": { // (3)!
    "granularity": "month",
    "groups": ["activity", "flow"],
    "since": "2026-08-01",
    "until": "2026-10-31",
    "by_author": false,
    "tz": "UTC",
    "settings": {
      "bot_logins": ["dependabot[bot]", "renovate[bot]"],
      "deploy_workflow": null,
      "exclude_merge_commits": true,
      "failure_window": "604800s",
      "hotfix_labels": ["hotfix"]
    }
  },
  "since": "2026-08-01", // (4)!
  "until": "2026-10-31",
  "series": [ // (5)!
    {
      "metric": "commits",
      "unit": "count",
      "by": null, // (6)!
      "by_kind": null,
      "points": [
        {"label": "2026-08", "start": "2026-08-01", "value": 38},
        {"label": "2026-09", "start": "2026-09-01", "value": 27},
        {"label": "2026-10", "start": "2026-10-01", "value": 1}
      ]
    },
    {
      "metric": "time_to_merge_p50",
      "unit": "hours",
      "by": null,
      "by_kind": null,
      "points": [
        {"label": "2026-08", "start": "2026-08-01", "value": 31.13111111111111}, // (7)!
        ...
      ]
    },
    ...
  ],
  "tables": { // (8)!
    "top_contributors": [
      {"login": "Rowlando13", "commits": 37, "lines_added": 496, "lines_deleted": 443,
       "lines_net": 53, "active_days": 22},
      ...
    ],
    "unavailable": [] // (9)!
  },
  "provenance": { // (10)!
    "schema_version": "4",
    "wambatic_version": "0.1.0",
    "fetched_at:commits": "2026-11-01T08:31:29.956551+00:00",
    "computed_at": "2026-11-01T08:58:02.039231+00:00",
    "timezone": "UTC",
    "partial_buckets": "",
    ...
  }
}
  1. The version of this document format. It changes only when the shape does, so a script can check it before reading anything else.
  2. kind is user, org or repo. For a repository, login is the owner and name the repository. For a user or organisation name is null.
  3. What was asked for, after the defaults were filled in. settings holds the stats.* settings that shaped the numbers (the time zone is in tz), with durations written as <seconds>s.
  4. The range that was resolved, both days inclusive. With no --since it is the day the first period holding data starts.
  5. One entry for each metric of the requested groups, in the order of the metrics reference.
  6. by and by_kind are both null for a total series. With --by-author a series has by_kind author and by the login. An organisation or user target also has per-repository series, with by_kind repo and by the owner/name.
  7. Values are integers for the units count, days and lines, and numbers with a fraction for the rest. A period with no value has no point at all: look for the label, do not expect a null.
  8. Tables over the whole range. top_contributors is always present; popularity and languages appear with the popularity group.
  9. Metrics whose inputs are not in the cache, each as {"metric", "reason"}. See Delivery and DORA.
  10. Where the data came from: the cache schema and wambatic versions, a fetched_at: time for each kind of record, a query: hash for each GraphQL query, and computed_at. partial_buckets lists the labels of the partial periods, joined by commas.

docs.title: jq recipes
docs.text:
These use jq. Each was run against the document above, extended to the activity, flow, delivery and popularity groups where a recipe needs them.

The points of one metric, as label value lines:

wambatic report repo:pallets/click --format json |
  jq -r '.series[] | select(.metric == "commits") | .points[] | "\(.label) \(.value)"'

The busiest period for a metric:

wambatic report repo:pallets/click --format json |
  jq '.series[] | select(.metric == "commits") | .points | max_by(.value)'

Every metric's most recent point:

wambatic report repo:pallets/click --format json |
  jq -r '.series[] | select(.by == null) | "\(.metric)\t\(.points[-1].label)\t\(.points[-1].value)"'

The top five contributors:

wambatic report org:pallets --format json |
  jq -r '.tables.top_contributors[:5][] | "\(.login)\t\(.commits)"'

Each author's commits in the range, with --by-author:

wambatic report org:pallets --by-author --format json |
  jq -r '.series[] | select(.by_kind == "author" and .metric == "commits")
         | "\(.by)\t\([.points[].value] | add)"'

The metrics that could not be computed, and why:

wambatic report repo:pallets/click --groups delivery --format json |
  jq -r '.tables.unavailable[] | "\(.metric): \(.reason)"'

When the data was last read from GitHub:

wambatic report repo:pallets/click --format json |
  jq -r '.provenance | to_entries[] | select(.key | startswith("fetched_at:")) | "\(.key) \(.value)"'

docs.title: Periods and ranges
docs.text:
How wambatic cuts a date range into periods, and what a partial period is.

wambatic report repo:pallets/click --by week --since 2026-09-01 --until 2026-10-15 --tz Europe/Berlin

docs.title: The options
docs.text:
Option Default Meaning --by year\|month\|week\|day\|total month The period to bucket by --since YYYY-MM-DD the first commit First day, inclusive, in the report time zone; not before 2008-01-01 --until YYYY-MM-DD today Last day, inclusive, in the report time zone; not after tomorrow in that zone --tz ZONE stats.timezone (UTC) An IANA time zone such as Europe/Berlin

--by total gives one row for the whole range, so there are no trends to draw and the HTML report rejects it: its tiles already show the totals.

Weeks are ISO weeks: they start on Monday, and a week belongs to the year that holds its Thursday, so the first days of January can fall in the last week of the previous year.

docs.title: The time zone
docs.text: Every event is placed in the period of its own date in the report time zone. A commit made at 23:30 UTC on 31 October is in October with --tz UTC and in November with --tz Europe/Berlin. The same holds for the first and last day of the range: --since and --until are days in that zone. An unknown zone is an error.

docs.title: Commits in their authors' zones
docs.text:
By default (--commit-tz report, or stats.commit_timezone set to report) a commit is dated in the report zone like every other event. With --commit-tz author each commit is dated on the calendar its author saw, and every other record (pull requests, issues, releases, runs) stays in the report zone.

A commit's author zone is the first of these that applies:

  1. the zone stats.author_timezones gives for the author's login (see Configuration);
  2. the UTC offset git recorded when the commit was made, for a repository read by clone;
  3. the report zone.

For example, a commit made on Monday 2 November at 01:00 +09:00 is stored as Sunday 1 November 16:00 UTC. In a UTC report it is on Sunday by default and on Monday with --commit-tz author, and it is inside --since 2026-11-02 only in the second case. Bucket labels, the partial-period marks and every series that is not made of commits are unchanged, and the default until is still today in the report zone.

GitHub's API gives commit times in UTC without the author's offset, so a repository that is not cloned has no offset. Its commits are dated in the report zone, unless stats.author_timezones names the author, and the report lists the repository in its unavailable section as commit dates: owner/name. The report title names both zones: "commits in authors' zones, other events in" the report zone.

docs.title: Partial periods
docs.text:
A range rarely starts on the first day of a period or ends on the last. The first and last periods are then partial: they hold only part of a period's days, so they look small next to the whole ones. wambatic marks them so you do not read a drop into the trend.

gantt
    title --since 2024-11-15 --until 2025-02-10 --by month
    dateFormat YYYY-MM-DD
    axisFormat %d %b
    section Range
    The range                 :active, 2024-11-15, 2025-02-10
    section Periods
    2024-11* (partial)        :crit, 2024-11-15, 2024-11-30
    2024-12                   :2024-12-01, 2024-12-31
    2025-01                   :2025-01-01, 2025-01-31
    2025-02* (partial)        :crit, 2025-02-01, 2025-02-10
  • In the terminal report a partial period ends in *, and the caption under the table says so.
  • In the HTML report a partial period is hatched in bar charts, drawn with open markers in line charts, and named in the chart's caption.
  • In the JSON output the provenance lists them under partial_buckets, as the period labels joined by commas; see JSON output.

If you want only whole periods, choose --since and --until that fall on period boundaries.

docs.title: Popularity
docs.text:
Stars, forks, watchers and languages: how a project is growing, and what it is written in.

wambatic report org:pallets --groups popularity

popularity is not in the default groups, because the first sync reads every star and every fork. Add it with --groups, for instance --groups activity,flow,delivery,popularity for everything.

Metric What it is stars_added Stars given in the period, by the date they were given stars_total The stars that exist now, counted by when they were given, up to the end of the period forks_added Direct forks made in the period, by the date they were made forks_total The forks that exist now, counted by when they were made, up to the end of the period

See the metrics reference for the definitions.

docs.title: The totals are cumulative
docs.text: A period's total is the events before the range plus those up to the end of the period, so totals do not add up over periods. They count what exists now: a star that was later removed is in none of them.

docs.title: The charts
docs.text: The HTML report draws the added and total series as charts. In this capture the star charts are flat at zero: GitHub did not list the stargazers to the token that made it, so there was no star history (see the last section). The fork charts show the series as they are drawn when the data exists.

docs.title: Popularity now and languages
docs.text:
Two tables go with the series.

Popularity now lists GitHub's own star, fork and watcher counts for each repository at the last sync, most starred first. The fork count is the whole network. Watchers exist only as this current count: GitHub does not say when anyone started watching.

Languages adds up the bytes of the largest languages GitHub reports for each repository, shown as a share of the total. With more than ten languages the table and the chart show the largest nine and one Other row for the rest; the JSON output has every row. It is a snapshot of the last sync, not a history.

docs.title: The cost of the first sync
docs.text:
The first sync with --groups popularity reads every star, newest first, about one request for each hundred, and lists every fork the same way, so a popular repository costs many requests against your rate limit. Later syncs compare the listed counts with the cache and read only the newer events. A count that has fallen (a star removed, a fork deleted) makes wambatic read that repository's stars or forks again from the start.

If GitHub will not list the stargazers to your token, the star series are left out and the Unavailable section says why; the star count under Popularity now is still shown. See Troubleshooting.

For a user target, every star and fork of the user's own repositories counts.

docs.title: Recipes
docs.text: Common workflows, ready to copy. Replace the names with your own.

docs.title: Reports from the terminal
docs.text:
# Sync only if the cache is more than a day old
wambatic report org:github --max-age 1d

# How a repository ships: runs, releases and the DORA proxies
wambatic report repo:OWNER/NAME --groups delivery

# How a project is growing: stars, forks and languages
wambatic report org:NAME --groups popularity

# Who did the work in an organisation
wambatic report org:github --by-author --since 2026-01-01

# One bucket for the whole range, in another time zone
wambatic report user:octocat --by total --tz Europe/Berlin

# Read all the history again, for example after a force-push you suspect
wambatic report repo:octocat/Hello-World --full-refresh

docs.title: A file to share
docs.text:
# An HTML page and its assets folder, opening on the week view, written to a file of your choice
wambatic report org:github --format html --by week --out reports/github.html

docs.title: Machine-readable output
docs.text:
# Logs stay on stderr, so the JSON can be piped
wambatic report org:github --format json | jq '.series[0].points'

See JSON output and the jq manual.

docs.title: An offline report from the cache
docs.text:
Sync while you have a network and a token, then report without either, for instance on a laptop on a train.

# Online: bring the cache up to date
wambatic report repo:octocat/Hello-World

# Offline: no network, no token
wambatic report repo:octocat/Hello-World --no-fetch

--no-fetch needs user:NAME, org:NAME or repo:OWNER/NAME, because a bare NAME is resolved with the network. If the cache holds nothing for the subject or the range, the report says so and suggests a sync.

docs.title: A nightly HTML report with cron
docs.text:
# crontab -e: every night at 02:30, write the report to a fixed file
30 2 * * * GITHUB_TOKEN=<token> /path/to/wambatic/.venv/bin/wambatic -q report org:NAME --format html --out /var/reports/NAME.html

cron runs with a bare environment, so give the full path to wambatic, set GITHUB_TOKEN (see The GitHub token; keep the crontab private, because the token sits in it) and use -q so only warnings and errors are mailed. <token> is a personal access token from https://github.com/settings/tokens. Because only what is new is fetched, a nightly run is cheap.

The exit status says whether it worked: see Exit statuses.

docs.title: Targets
docs.text:
How to name the user, organisation or repository to report on.

wambatic report org:pallets

The first argument of report and serve is the target. It says which repositories wambatic reads from GitHub and reports on.

Target Meaning user:NAME The repositories owned by a user, counting only that user's own commits org:NAME The repositories owned by an organisation repo:OWNER/NAME or OWNER/NAME One repository NAME Asks GitHub whether NAME is a user or an organisation

Prefixes are lower case. A user, organisation or owner NAME is 1 to 39 letters, digits and -; a repository NAME is 1 to 100 letters, digits, ., _ and -. A malformed target is an error before anything is fetched.

docs.title: From a target to the repositories that are read
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    T[target] --> P{prefix?}
    P -->|"repo: or OWNER/NAME"| R[that one repository]
    P -->|"user:"| U[list the user's repositories]
    P -->|"org:"| O[list the organisation's repositories]
    P -->|"bare NAME"| Q["ask GitHub: user or organisation?<br/>(one request)"]
    Q -->|user| U
    Q -->|organisation| O
    U --> F{"fork or archived?"}
    O --> F
    F -->|"no"| K[read it]
    F -->|"yes, and fetch.include_forks<br/>or fetch.include_archived is set"| K
    F -->|"yes, otherwise"| S[left out]
    R --> K

docs.title: What each target counts
docs.text:
A repository (repo:pallets/click, or just pallets/click) reports on that repository alone. Naming it directly always reads it, even if it is a fork or archived: you asked for it.

An organisation (org:pallets) reports on every repository the organisation owns. The report has a By repository table that splits the totals by repository; add --by-author for a By author table too.

A user (user:octocat) reports on the repositories the user owns, and counts only commits made by that user. --by-author is not available for a user target, because every commit counted is already the user's.

A bare name (octocat) costs one request to find out which of the two it is, so it cannot be used with --no-fetch, which makes no request at all. Use user: or org: there. Prefer the prefix in scripts too: it saves the request and says what you meant.

docs.title: Forks and archived repositories
docs.text: A user or organisation target leaves out forks and archived repositories, since their history is usually someone else's. To include them, set fetch.include_forks or fetch.include_archived in the configuration; see Settings for their defaults.

docs.title: Private repositories
docs.text: A target that names private repositories needs a token that can read them; see The GitHub token for the scopes.

docs.title: The terminal report
docs.text:
Every section of the default report, in the order it is printed.

wambatic report repo:pallets/click --by month --groups activity,flow,delivery,popularity

--format terminal is the default. The screenshots below were made with all four metric groups; the default groups, activity,flow, print fewer sections.

Note

Screenshots captured on 2026-11-11 from pallets/click and org:pallets with wambatic 0.1.0, covering 2024-11-01 to 2026-10-31.

docs.title: Sections in output order
docs.text:
1. A title line with the subject, the date range, the period and the time zone.
  2. Activity by period: commits, contributors, active days, and lines added, deleted and net for each period, with a Total row when there is more than one period.
  3. Trends, when there is more than one period (so not with --by total).
  4. By repository for a user or organisation, and By author with --by-author.
  5. Top contributors, the first rows only.
  6. Flow by period and Flow times by period.
  7. With --groups delivery: Delivery by period and DORA proxies by period.
  8. With --groups popularity: Popularity by period, Popularity now and Languages.
  9. Unavailable: metrics whose inputs are not in the cache, with the reason.
  10. Provenance: where the data came from.

docs.title: Title and Activity by period
docs.text: A period that the range cuts short ends in *; the caption under the table explains it. See Periods and ranges and Activity.

docs.title: Trends and the tables that follow
docs.text:
Trends draws a sparkline for each metric that has a value in every period, cropped to the width of your terminal, with the lowest and highest value beside it. The tables after it are Top contributors, Flow, Delivery and DORA and Popularity, each as a table with one row for each period.

Top contributors lists only the first rows and ends with "and N more"; the JSON output has every row.

docs.title: By repository and By author
docs.text:
An organisation or user target adds a By repository table, and --by-author adds By author:

wambatic report org:pallets --by-author

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text: Read this when two reports disagree: the fetch times tell you which one saw newer data. The wambatic and cache schema versions are listed here too.

docs.title: Colour and width
docs.text: Nothing in the output depends on colour: net lines carry an explicit sign, - stands for a period with no value, and partial periods carry a *. Sparklines are cropped to the terminal width, so a narrow terminal shows fewer periods of them, not a broken layout. When stdout is not a terminal, for instance in a pipe or a file, wambatic writes plain text without colour codes.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Each error wambatic prints, and what to do about it.

wambatic prints one line to stderr and exits with a status that tells the kind of failure (see Exit statuses). Add -v for debugging detail. The messages below are quoted from the program; a ... stands for a value that varies.

docs.title: Token and access
docs.text: Message What to do No GitHub token found: set GITHUB_TOKEN or run gh auth login Set GITHUB_TOKEN or sign in with the GitHub CLI. See The GitHub token. A report from the cache with --no-fetch needs none GitHub rejected the token (401) The token is wrong, expired or revoked. Create a new one and set GITHUB_TOKEN GitHub denied access (403), perhaps with the endpoint accepts scopes: ... The token lacks a scope or permission. Use repo for private repositories and read:org for private organisation membership, or the permissions listed on the token page. A fine-grained token reaches only the repositories selected when it was made ... not found or not visible, ... not found or ... is not a user or an organisation Check the spelling of the target, and that the token can see a private repository

docs.title: Rate limits and slow syncs
docs.text:
Message What to do GitHub rate limit exhausted; resets at ... The limit is used up until the time shown, in UTC. Wait until then; with fetch.on_rate_limit set to fail wambatic stops with this message, while the default wait sleeps until the reset. Report from the cache meanwhile with --no-fetch. The message also appears when wait gives up after fetch.max_retries retries of a secondary limit; lower fetch.workers to stay clear of those GitHub is still computing ...; try again later GitHub builds some statistics on request. Run the report again in a minute. fetch.stats_retries sets how long wambatic waits GitHub answered HTTP ... to ... or GitHub request ... failed: ... GitHub or the network failed after the retries. Run it again; what was already fetched is kept

A first sync of a large target is slow, because it reads the whole history: about one request for each hundred commits, runs, stars or forks. Later syncs read only what is new. delivery and popularity are the costly groups, so leave them out of --groups if you do not need them. See The cache.

With --no-fetch, run once without it to fill the cache; otherwise widen --since and --until

docs.title: The web app
docs.text:
Running the local web app and using its form, pages and GraphQL API.

wambatic serve octocat

This starts a web app on your machine and logs the address, http://127.0.0.1:8000/, and the URL of the report for the target you gave. The target is optional: it only fills in the form. Submitting the form shows the same page as report --format html, on the same cache.

Note

Screenshots captured on 2026-11-11 from pallets/click and org:pallets with wambatic 0.1.0, covering 2024-11-01 to 2026-10-31.

docs.title: The progress page
docs.text:
A report that needs a sync does not make the browser wait for it. The server answers at once with a progress page that shows the state, how many repositories are done and how many rows were written, polls once a second, and loads the report when the sync is done.

A large organisation can take minutes; the rest of the app stays responsive meanwhile. One sync runs at a time, so a second target waits its turn, and asking again for a target that is already syncing joins its sync. If a sync fails, the page shows the message and a link to try again.

A job is in one of these states:

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> queued: request needs a sync
    queued --> listing: no other sync is running
    listing --> syncing: repository listing read
    syncing --> done
    listing --> failed
    syncing --> failed
    done --> [*]
    failed --> [*]

The progress page words queued as "Waiting for another sync to finish" and syncing as "Syncing repositories".

docs.title: Commit dates
docs.text: The form has a "Commit dates" select: the report zone, or each commit's author's zone. It is preset from stats.commit_timezone, and is sent as commit_tz, which the stats query takes too. See Periods.

docs.title: How fresh is fresh
docs.text: The web app syncs on the same rule as report: --max-age (or fetch.max_age) says how recent a sync may be to skip the network. The default is zero, so every page you open syncs first. For a server you leave running, wambatic serve --max-age 1h is usually what you want. A page you reach from the progress page does not sync a second time.

docs.title: The GraphQL API
docs.text:
/graphql is the API of the app. It has a stats query, a sync mutation and a job query. The stats input takes the same parameters as the report (target, by, since, until, groups, by_author, tz, commit_tz, and job) and returns what report --format json prints, as typed fields (subject, request, series) and as JSON for tables and provenance. by is TOTAL, YEAR, MONTH, WEEK or DAY; TOTAL is allowed here.

stats never starts a sync. When the cache is older than fetch.max_age, it answers SyncNeeded; you start the sync with the sync mutation, poll job until its state is DONE, and ask stats again with the job's id as job:

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client (curl)
    participant S as wambatic serve
    C->>S: query stats
    S-->>C: SyncNeeded
    C->>S: mutation sync
    S-->>C: job id
    loop until state is DONE
        C->>S: query job
        S-->>C: state, repos_done, rows_written
    end
    C->>S: query stats with job
    S-->>C: the statistics

A POST must declare Content-Type: application/json; anything else is refused with 415. Without that rule a web page on another site could send a form-encoded request that a browser makes without asking first, and start a sync with your token.

# 1. Ask for statistics. A cold cache answers SyncNeeded.
curl -s -H 'Content-Type: application/json' http://127.0.0.1:8000/graphql -d '{
  "query": "query($i: StatsInput!) { stats(input: $i) { __typename ... on SyncNeeded { message } ... on Stats { since until } } }",
  "variables": {"i": {"target": "repo:octocat/Hello-World", "by": "WEEK"}}}'

# 2. Start the sync.
curl -s -H 'Content-Type: application/json' http://127.0.0.1:8000/graphql -d '{
  "query": "mutation($i: StatsInput!) { sync(input: $i) { id state } }",
  "variables": {"i": {"target": "repo:octocat/Hello-World", "by": "WEEK"}}}'
# {"data": {"sync": {"id": "9c1b...", "state": "QUEUED"}}}

# 3. Poll the job until its state is DONE.
curl -s -H 'Content-Type: application/json' http://127.0.0.1:8000/graphql -d '{
  "query": "{ job(id: \"9c1b...\") { state reposDone reposListed rowsWritten error } }"}'

# 4. Ask again with the job.
curl -s -H 'Content-Type: application/json' http://127.0.0.1:8000/graphql -d '{
  "query": "query($i: StatsInput!) { stats(input: $i) { ... on Stats { since until series(metrics: [\"commits\"]) { metric points { label value } } } } }",
  "variables": {"i": {"target": "repo:octocat/Hello-World", "by": "WEEK", "job": "9c1b..."}}}'

A failure is a GraphQL error with an extensions.code and extensions.status:

Code Status Meaning BAD_REQUEST 400 A bad parameter NOT_FOUND 404 A target that does not exist, or has nothing in range UPSTREAM 502 A GitHub error, for example no token INTERNAL 500 Anything unexpected; the details are in the server's log BAD_QUERY none A query that does not match the schema

The report pages show the same errors as a short page. See JSON output for the document.

docs.title: GraphiQL
docs.text: Opening /graphql in a browser shows GraphiQL, an editor for trying queries, with the schema beside it. It loads its script and style from jsDelivr, so unlike the other pages it needs a network connection. The curl calls above do not.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
The server uses the GITHUB_TOKEN of the environment it runs in, and never sends it to the browser. It listens on loopback only, and refuses any other address unless you pass --allow-remote (or set report.allow_remote), because anyone who can reach the port can then read whatever your token can read, private repositories included, and make wambatic spend your rate limit. On loopback it also answers 403 to a request whose Host header is not localhost, 127.0.0.1 or [::1] with the port the server listens on, which stops a web page on another site from reaching it through DNS rebinding. That check is off with --allow-remote, since the names the server is reached by are not known. The app sends no CORS headers, so other sites cannot read its answers.

flowchart TD
    A[request arrives] --> B{"listening on loopback<br/>(no --allow-remote)?"}
    B -->|no| OK[handle the request]
    B -->|yes| C{"Host is localhost, 127.0.0.1 or [::1]<br/>with the server's port?"}
    C -->|yes| OK
    C -->|no| X["403 unexpected Host header"]

docs.text: Global options come before the command, as for report: wambatic -v serve .... The full table is in Command line.

docs.title: Stopping
docs.text: Press Ctrl-C. A running sync is cancelled and resumes where it stopped on the next sync, and the exit status is 130.
